items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "political context".
items.answer: The impacts of digital systems on power, government, elections, law and civic participation
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the impacts of digital systems on power, government, elections, law and civic participation. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between the social context and the cultural context.
items.answer: The social context focuses on relationships, communities and social groups (e.g. online friendships, inequality); the cultural context focuses on arts, traditions, languages and shared meanings (e.g. memes, heritage digitisation).
items.markingKey: The social context focuses on relationships, communities and social groups (e.g. online friendships, inequality); the cultural context focuses on arts, traditions, languages and shared meanings (e.g. memes, heritage digitisation). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The environmental context only covers climate change." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It also covers e-waste, mining of minerals, water use by data centres, biodiversity monitoring and the use of technology for environmental protection.
items.markingKey: It also covers e-waste, mining of minerals, water use by data centres, biodiversity monitoring and the use of technology for environmental protection. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Telemedicine means my father no longer travels four hours to see a specialist – when the network works."
— Resident of a rural district in Peru, 2023

Explain which two contexts the source illustrates.
items.answer: Health (access to specialist care) and social/economic (reduced travel time and cost, but unequal connectivity – the digital divide).
items.markingKey: Health (access to specialist care) and social/economic (reduced travel time and cost, but unequal connectivity – the digital divide). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which Digital Society context does the following example most directly fit? Example: micro-targeted political adverts during an election campaign.
items.answer: political
items.markingKey: D. Best fit is the political context because it concerns power, elections and governance; examples can involve several contexts.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Digital technology has had a more positive impact in the health context than in any other context."
items.answer: Health shows strong benefits, but they are uneven and matched by new harms; comparisons across contexts depend on the criteria used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: telemedicine, wearables and digital records improve access and care; disease surveillance and research. Arguments against: mental-health harms from social media; health-data privacy breaches; unequal access. Supported judgement: Health shows strong benefits, but they are uneven and matched by new harms; comparisons across contexts depend on the criteria used.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "environmental context"?
options: Relevant information, examples and concepts that a student brings from outside the sources provided
The impacts of digital systems on work, business, markets, trade and income
The impacts of digital systems on physical and mental well-being and on health care
The impacts of digital systems on the natural world, resources, energy and climate
items.answer: The impacts of digital systems on the natural world, resources, energy and climate
items.markingKey: D. "environmental context" is the impacts of digital systems on the natural world, resources, energy and climate.

items.stem: Explain why contexts are useful for structuring a Digital Society inquiry.
items.answer: They help students identify which kinds of impacts and stakeholders to investigate, make comparisons across examples and avoid looking only at technical features.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They help students identify which kinds of impacts and stakeholders to investigate, make comparisons across examples and avoid looking only at technical features. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to eSanjeevani in India, explain how it illustrates the health context.
items.answer: India's national telemedicine service eSanjeevani had recorded well over 100 million consultations by 2023, connecting rural patients with doctors remotely. Remote consultations widened access to care for rural patients, though connectivity and digital literacy limited who benefited.
items.markingKey: Context (India's national telemedicine service eSanjeevani had recorded well over 100 million consultations by 2023, connecting rural patients with doctors remotely.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: remote consultations widened access to care for rural patients, though connectivity and digital literacy limited who benefited. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the health context.

items.stem: Choose one real-world digital system and analyse its impacts in three different contexts.
items.answer: Select a specific system (e.g. TikTok, M-Pesa, Aadhaar, a smart-city project); analyse impacts in three contexts with evidence; show interactions between contexts; conclude on overall significance.
items.markingKey: Select a specific system (e.g. TikTok, M-Pesa, Aadhaar, a smart-city project); analyse impacts in three contexts with evidence; show interactions between contexts; conclude on overall significance.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "own knowledge"?
options: The impacts of digital systems on power, government, elections, law and civic participation
To confirm a claim by finding support for it in another independent source
Relevant information, examples and concepts that a student brings from outside the sources provided
The impacts of digital systems on how knowledge is created, shared, stored and judged reliable
items.answer: Relevant information, examples and concepts that a student brings from outside the sources provided
items.markingKey: C. "own knowledge" is relevant information, examples and concepts that a student brings from outside the sources provided.

items.stem: "Comparing two sources means describing each one in turn." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Strong comparison links the sources point by point (running comparison) and explains similarities and differences, rather than writing two separate summaries.
items.markingKey: Strong comparison links the sources point by point (running comparison) and explains similarities and differences, rather than writing two separate summaries. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between evidence in a source and a claim in a source.
items.answer: A claim is what the source asserts (e.g. "AI will destroy jobs"); evidence is the data or examples it offers to support that claim (e.g. a survey of employers).
items.markingKey: A claim is what the source asserts (e.g. "AI will destroy jobs"); evidence is the data or examples it offers to support that claim (e.g. a survey of employers). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Our AI tutor improved test scores by 30% in a pilot of 200 students."
— Press release by an educational technology company, 2024

Analyse one value and one limitation of this source for an inquiry into AI in education.
items.answer: Value: shows the company's claimed outcomes and how it markets its product. Limitation: produced by the company (promotional purpose), small pilot, no information on control group, independence or which tests – needs corroboration.
items.markingKey: Value: shows the company's claimed outcomes and how it markets its product. Limitation: produced by the company (promotional purpose), small pilot, no information on control group, independence or which tests – needs corroboration. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
Source (data): Share of the world population using the internet (ITU, approximate)
2005: 16
2015: 41
2024: 68

Calculate the percentage change between 2005 and 2015. Identify one limitation of using this source on its own to make claims about digital society.
items.answer: 156.2%; e.g. it shows only one indicator and does not explain causes, who is included/excluded, or how the data was collected
items.markingKey: (41 − 16) ÷ 16 × 100 = 156.2% [M1 A1]. Limitation: aggregate figures hide inequalities, no information on methodology or causes, single indicator [R1 R1].

items.stem: With reference to the COMPAS debate between ProPublica and Northpointe, explain how it illustrates comparing sources that use different evidence.
items.answer: ProPublica (2016) argued COMPAS was biased because of unequal false positive rates; Northpointe replied it was fair because scores were equally calibrated across groups. The sources reach opposite conclusions partly because they use different fairness definitions, showing why students must analyse how each source defines and measures its claims.
items.markingKey: Context (ProPublica (2016) argued COMPAS was biased because of unequal false positive rates; Northpointe replied it was fair because scores were equally calibrated across groups.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the sources reach opposite conclusions partly because they use different fairness definitions, showing why students must analyse how each source defines and measures its claims. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to comparing sources that use different evidence.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Primary sources are more useful than secondary sources for Paper 2-style analysis."
items.answer: Usefulness depends on the question; strong answers combine primary evidence with secondary context and own knowledge.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: first-hand evidence of stakeholder views and data; allow students to make their own interpretations. Arguments against: secondary sources provide context, synthesis and expert analysis; primary sources can be narrow, biased or unrepresentative. Supported judgement: Usefulness depends on the question; strong answers combine primary evidence with secondary context and own knowledge.

items.stem: "Statistical sources are more reliable than personal testimony." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Statistics show scale and testimony shows experience; reliability depends on method and origin, not type.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: represent many cases and show scale; less influenced by individual emotion. Arguments against: statistics depend on definitions and collection methods; can be selectively presented; testimony captures experiences and causes statistics miss. Supported judgement: Statistics show scale and testimony shows experience; reliability depends on method and origin, not type. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Define the term "compare and contrast".
items.answer: IB command term: give an account of similarities and differences between two or more items, referring to both throughout
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: IB command term: give an account of similarities and differences between two or more items, referring to both throughout. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why answers to evaluation questions in Paper 2 should use both the sources and own knowledge.
items.answer: The sources give specific evidence to analyse, while own knowledge adds wider examples, context and counter-arguments; together they allow a balanced, well-supported judgement, which markbands reward.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The sources give specific evidence to analyse, while own knowledge adds wider examples, context and counter-arguments; together they allow a balanced, well-supported judgement, which markbands reward. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why visual sources such as cartoons need careful interpretation.
items.answer: Cartoons use symbols, exaggeration and irony to make an argument, so the reader must identify the message, the cartoonist's perspective and the context rather than reading it literally.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cartoons use symbols, exaggeration and irony to make an argument, so the reader must identify the message, the cartoonist's perspective and the context rather than reading it literally. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source (data): UPI transactions in India in December of each year (billions, NPCI)
2018: 0.62
2020: 2.23
2023: 12

Calculate the percentage change between 2018 and 2020. Identify one limitation of using this source on its own to make claims about digital society.
items.answer: 259.7%; e.g. it shows only one indicator and does not explain causes, who is included/excluded, or how the data was collected
items.markingKey: (2.23 − 0.62) ÷ 0.62 × 100 = 259.7% [M1 A1]. Limitation: aggregate figures hide inequalities, no information on methodology or causes, single indicator [R1 R1].

items.stem: Two sources disagree about whether TikTok harms teenagers' mental health: a TikTok safety blog post and a survey by a children's charity. Explain how you would compare and evaluate them to answer a Paper 2 question.
items.answer: Identify claims and evidence in each; analyse origin, purpose, methods (sample, questions); find similarities/differences; bring own knowledge (e.g. Facebook Files, US Surgeon General advisory 2023, research on correlation vs causation); reach a balanced judgement.
items.markingKey: Identify claims and evidence in each; analyse origin, purpose, methods (sample, questions); find similarities/differences; bring own knowledge (e.g. Facebook Files, US Surgeon General advisory 2023, research on correlation vs causation); reach a balanced judgement.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "to what extent"?
options: IB command term: consider the merits or otherwise of an argument or concept, with opinions and conclusions clearly presented and supported
The impacts of digital systems on the natural world, resources, energy and climate
To confirm a claim by finding support for it in another independent source
The impacts of digital systems on arts, traditions, languages, beliefs and identities
items.answer: IB command term: consider the merits or otherwise of an argument or concept, with opinions and conclusions clearly presented and supported
items.markingKey: A. "to what extent" is IB command term: consider the merits or otherwise of an argument or concept, with opinions and conclusions clearly presented and supported.

items.stem: Explain the difference between evaluate and explain.
items.answer: Explain asks for causes, reasons or mechanisms; evaluate asks for a judgement that weighs strengths and limitations.
items.markingKey: Explain asks for causes, reasons or mechanisms; evaluate asks for a judgement that weighs strengths and limitations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a conclusion should follow from the analysis.
items.answer: A judgement that weighs the evidence presented, rather than repeating the question or introducing new points, shows the reasoning behind the student's position, which is what evaluation questions assess.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A judgement that weighs the evidence presented, rather than repeating the question or introducing new points, shows the reasoning behind the student's position, which is what evaluation questions assess. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Uber v Aslam (UK Supreme Court, 2021), explain how it illustrates power and the economic context of platforms.
items.answer: The UK Supreme Court ruled in February 2021 that Uber drivers were "workers" entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay, not self-employed contractors. The ruling shows how courts can rebalance power between platforms and workers, and how algorithmic management (pay, ratings) shaped the legal decision.
items.markingKey: Context (The UK Supreme Court ruled in February 2021 that Uber drivers were "workers" entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay, not self-employed contractors.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the ruling shows how courts can rebalance power between platforms and workers, and how algorithmic management (pay, ratings) shaped the legal decision. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to power and the economic context of platforms.

items.stem: "A balanced answer should avoid reaching a conclusion." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Balance means considering different perspectives, but evaluation questions require a clear, supported judgement.
items.markingKey: Balance means considering different perspectives, but evaluation questions require a clear, supported judgement. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Uber drivers are workers, not independent contractors."
— Summary of the UK Supreme Court judgment in Uber BV v Aslam, February 2021

Explain how this source could be used in a Paper 1 answer about power.
items.answer: It shows a legal intervention that limited platform power over workers, providing a specific example of resistance and regulation in the economic context.
items.markingKey: It shows a legal intervention that limited platform power over workers, providing a specific example of resistance and regulation in the economic context. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to one real-world example, evaluate the impact of a digital system on one group of stakeholders, linking at least one concept and one context.
items.answer: Specific example (e.g. Uber drivers, Aadhaar welfare recipients, A-level students in 2020); concept (power, identity, values) and context (economic, political, social); impacts with evidence; implications; balanced judgement.
items.markingKey: Specific example (e.g. Uber drivers, Aadhaar welfare recipients, A-level students in 2020); concept (power, identity, values) and context (economic, political, social); impacts with evidence; implications; balanced judgement.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the use of algorithms in education does more harm than good.
items.answer: Algorithms can support learning when used transparently with human oversight; harm arises when they make high-stakes decisions without accountability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Ofqual 2020 downgrading; proctoring software errors and privacy invasion. Arguments against: adaptive learning platforms personalise practice; automated feedback saves teachers time. Supported judgement: Algorithms can support learning when used transparently with human oversight; harm arises when they make high-stakes decisions without accountability. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Explain why analysing impacts on different stakeholders strengthens an answer.
items.answer: It shows that a digital system creates winners and losers, reveals power relations and makes evaluation balanced rather than one-sided.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It shows that a digital system creates winners and losers, reveals power relations and makes evaluation balanced rather than one-sided. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Balance means considering different perspectives, but evaluation questions require a clear, supported judgement.

items.markingKey: Context (The UK Supreme Court ruled in February 2021 that Uber drivers were "workers" entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay, not self-employed contractors.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Ditch the algorithm!"
— Chant by students protesting outside the Department for Education, London, August 2020

Explain what the source reveals about public attitudes to algorithmic decision-making.
items.answer: Students rejected an algorithm deciding their futures, showing distrust of opaque automated decisions and a demand for human, individual judgement and accountability.
items.markingKey: Students rejected an algorithm deciding their futures, showing distrust of opaque automated decisions and a demand for human, individual judgement and accountability. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "What a source is useful for in answering a specific question, given its origin, purpose and content"?
items.answer: value (of a source)
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of value (of a source).

items.stem: Define the term "evaluate".
items.answer: IB command term: make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: IB command term: make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The impacts of digital systems on how knowledge is created, shared, stored and judged reliable"?
items.answer: human knowledge context
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of human knowledge context.

items.stem: "A biased source should be ignored in Paper 2." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Biased sources are often valuable for showing a stakeholder's perspective; the skill is to recognise the bias and evaluate the source in that light.
items.markingKey: Biased sources are often valuable for showing a stakeholder's perspective; the skill is to recognise the bias and evaluate the source in that light. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between describing an example and analysing an example.
items.answer: Describing tells what happened (Robodebt sent debt letters); analysing explains why and how it matters, linking to concepts and stakeholders (automated averaging shifted the burden of proof onto vulnerable people, showing power and values issues).
items.markingKey: Describing tells what happened (Robodebt sent debt letters); analysing explains why and how it matters, linking to concepts and stakeholders (automated averaging shifted the burden of proof onto vulnerable people, showing power and values issues). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Each real-world example belongs to only one context." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most examples cut across several contexts; students choose the most relevant ones for their focus and can analyse interactions between them.
items.markingKey: Most examples cut across several contexts; students choose the most relevant ones for their focus and can analyse interactions between them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Explain asks for causes, reasons or mechanisms; evaluate asks for a judgement that weighs strengths and limitations.
items.markingKey: Explain asks for causes, reasons or mechanisms; evaluate asks for a judgement that weighs strengths and limitations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the political context and the economic context.
items.answer: The economic context concerns work, markets and income (e.g. gig work pay); the political context concerns power, law and government (e.g. laws regulating gig platforms).
items.markingKey: The economic context concerns work, markets and income (e.g. gig work pay); the political context concerns power, law and government (e.g. laws regulating gig platforms). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe Meta's transparency reports versus whistle-blower evidence and explain what it reveals about origin and purpose of sources.
items.answer: Meta's reports present high proactive detection rates for harmful content, while Frances Haugen's 2021 disclosures suggested internal research showed only a small share of hate speech was removed. The company's public reports and internal documents serve different purposes, so evaluating claims requires comparing origin, purpose and evidence.
items.markingKey: Context (Meta's reports present high proactive detection rates for harmful content, while Frances Haugen's 2021 disclosures suggested internal research showed only a small share of hate speech was removed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the company's public reports and internal documents serve different purposes, so evaluating claims requires comparing origin, purpose and evidence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to origin and purpose of sources.

items.stem: With reference to Ofqual's 2020 grading algorithm, explain how it illustrates applying concepts, content and contexts.
items.answer: With exams cancelled, an algorithm adjusted teacher grades using schools' historical results; about 39% of grades were lowered and after protests ("Ditch the algorithm") the government reverted to teacher grades. The case links algorithms (content), power and values (concepts) and education/political contexts, making it a strong Paper 1 example.
items.markingKey: Context (With exams cancelled, an algorithm adjusted teacher grades using schools' historical results; about 39% of grades were lowered and after protests ("Ditch the algorithm") the government reverted to teacher grades.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case links algorithms (content), power and values (concepts) and education/political contexts, making it a strong Paper 1 example. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to applying concepts, content and contexts.

items.stem: Identify two Digital Society contexts relevant to the following example and explain why each applies: TikTok creators reviving interest in traditional Indigenous songs.
items.answer: Cultural (it concerns traditions, language, arts and identity), plus one other justified context, e.g. social, economic or political implications
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each relevant context identified (the most direct is cultural); 1 mark for each explanation linking the example to that context. Accept any justified second context.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Children who use screens more than seven hours a day show thinning of the brain's cortex."
— Headline summarising early results from a US study of adolescent brain development, 2018

Explain why this source should be evaluated carefully before being used as evidence.
items.answer: A headline simplifies early findings; correlation does not show causation; the study's researchers cautioned against conclusions; the original study and later results should be checked.
items.markingKey: A headline simplifies early findings; correlation does not show causation; the study's researchers cautioned against conclusions; the original study and later results should be checked. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the TikTok ban debate in the USA shows power, space and political context.
items.answer: In 2024 the US passed a law requiring ByteDance to divest TikTok or face a ban, citing national-security concerns about data and influence; the Supreme Court upheld the law in January 2025. The case links data flows across borders, platform ownership and state power, illustrating multiple concepts in one example.
items.markingKey: Context (In 2024 the US passed a law requiring ByteDance to divest TikTok or face a ban, citing national-security concerns about data and influence; the Supreme Court upheld the law in January 2025.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case links data flows across borders, platform ownership and state power, illustrating multiple concepts in one example. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to power, space and political context.

items.stem: Using the digitisation of the Timbuktu manuscripts as an example, explain the cultural and human knowledge contexts.
items.answer: Projects with Google Arts & Culture and other partners digitised thousands of historic manuscripts from Timbuktu, Mali, some of which had been smuggled to safety in 2012–13. Digitisation preserves and shares cultural heritage globally, but raises questions about ownership and who controls access to the copies.
items.markingKey: Context (Projects with Google Arts & Culture and other partners digitised thousands of historic manuscripts from Timbuktu, Mali, some of which had been smuggled to safety in 2012–13.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: digitisation preserves and shares cultural heritage globally, but raises questions about ownership and who controls access to the copies. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the cultural and human knowledge contexts.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a cartoon about smartphone addiction shows interpreting visual sources.
items.answer: Cartoons often show families at a table all staring at phones to criticise the effect of devices on relationships. The image makes an argument through exaggeration; students should identify the message, consider the cartoonist's perspective and test it against research evidence.
items.markingKey: Context (Cartoons often show families at a table all staring at phones to criticise the effect of devices on relationships.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the image makes an argument through exaggeration; students should identify the message, consider the cartoonist's perspective and test it against research evidence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interpreting visual sources.

items.answer: Algorithms can support learning when used transparently with human oversight; harm arises when they make high-stakes decisions without accountability.

items.stem: "The economic context is the most important lens for understanding digital systems." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Economics is often central, but the most important lens depends on the example and inquiry focus; strong analysis connects several contexts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: digital systems are driven by business models and profit; economic impacts (jobs, income) affect all other areas. Arguments against: political, social and cultural impacts are not reducible to economics; some impacts (dignity, rights, knowledge) are non-economic; importance varies with the example. Supported judgement: Economics is often central, but the most important lens depends on the example and inquiry focus; strong analysis connects several contexts. items.stem: "Gig-economy platforms have given workers more freedom than traditional employment." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Platforms offer flexibility, but algorithmic control and weak protections mean freedom is often limited; regulation is reshaping the balance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flexible hours and easy entry to work; income opportunities for migrants and students. Arguments against: algorithmic management controls pay and access to jobs; lack of sick pay, pensions and protection; courts (Uber v Aslam) and the EU Platform Work Directive (2024) recognise imbalance. Supported judgement: Platforms offer flexibility, but algorithmic control and weak protections mean freedom is often limited; regulation is reshaping the balance. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: Which of the following is the best example of using "own knowledge" in an evaluation question?
options: Describing the layout of the source
Referring to the GDPR fine against Meta when evaluating a source about data protection
items.answer: Referring to the GDPR fine against Meta when evaluating a source about data protection

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "IB command term: consider the merits or otherwise of an argument or concept, with opinions and conclusions clearly presented and supported"?
items.answer: to what extent

items.stem: How many contexts are identified in the Digital Society guide?
items.answer: Seven
items.markingKey: Seven. Cultural, economic, environmental, health, human knowledge, political and social.

items.stem: Distinguish between the reliability of a source and the value of a source.
items.answer: Value is how useful a source is for a specific question (even a biased source can be valuable for showing a perspective); reliability is how far its information can be trusted as accurate.
items.markingKey: Value is how useful a source is for a specific question (even a biased source can be valuable for showing a perspective); reliability is how far its information can be trusted as accurate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between analysing an example and describing an example.
items.answer: Describing tells what happened (Robodebt sent debt letters); analysing explains why and how it matters, linking to concepts and stakeholders (automated averaging shifted the burden of proof onto vulnerable people, showing power and values issues).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the cultural context and the social context.
items.answer: The social context focuses on relationships, communities and social groups (e.g. online friendships, inequality); the cultural context focuses on arts, traditions, languages and shared meanings (e.g. memes, heritage digitisation).

items.stem: Lukas writes: "Each real-world example belongs to only one context." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most examples cut across several contexts; students choose the most relevant ones for their focus and can analyse interactions between them.
items.markingKey: Most examples cut across several contexts; students choose the most relevant ones for their focus and can analyse interactions between them. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Meta's transparency reports versus whistle-blower evidence as an example, explain origin and purpose of sources.
items.answer: Meta's reports present high proactive detection rates for harmful content, while Frances Haugen's 2021 disclosures suggested internal research showed only a small share of hate speech was removed. The company's public reports and internal documents serve different purposes, so evaluating claims requires comparing origin, purpose and evidence.
items.markingKey: Context (Meta's reports present high proactive detection rates for harmful content, while Frances Haugen's 2021 disclosures suggested internal research showed only a small share of hate speech was removed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the company's public reports and internal documents serve different purposes, so evaluating claims requires comparing origin, purpose and evidence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to origin and purpose of sources.

items.answer: Examples must be relevant, accurate and analysed; a few well-developed examples linked to the question score higher than a list of names.

items.stem: Which Digital Society context does the following example most directly fit? Example: TikTok creators reviving interest in traditional Indigenous songs.
items.answer: cultural
items.markingKey: A. Best fit is the cultural context because it concerns traditions, language, arts and identity; examples can involve several contexts.

items.stem:
Source (data): Share of adults in Kenya with a mobile-money account (World Bank Global Findex)
2014: 58
2017: 73
2021: 79

Calculate the percentage change between 2017 and 2021. Identify one limitation of using this source on its own to make claims about digital society.
items.answer: 8.2%; e.g. it shows only one indicator and does not explain causes, who is included/excluded, or how the data was collected
items.markingKey: (79 − 73) ÷ 73 × 100 = 8.2% [M1 A1]. Limitation: aggregate figures hide inequalities, no information on methodology or causes, single indicator [R1 R1].

items.stem: Identify two Digital Society contexts relevant to the following example and explain why each applies: ride-hailing platforms changing taxi drivers' incomes in Lagos.

2018: 0.62

Calculate the percentage change between 2020 and 2023. Identify one limitation of using this source on its own to make claims about digital society.
items.answer: 438.1%; e.g. it shows only one indicator and does not explain causes, who is included/excluded, or how the data was collected

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The use of algorithms in education does more harm than good."
items.answer: Algorithms can support learning when used transparently with human oversight; harm arises when they make high-stakes decisions without accountability.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Ofqual 2020 downgrading; proctoring software errors and privacy invasion. Arguments against: adaptive learning platforms personalise practice; automated feedback saves teachers time. Supported judgement: Algorithms can support learning when used transparently with human oversight; harm arises when they make high-stakes decisions without accountability.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Digital technology has had a more positive impact in the health context than in any other context."
items.answer: Health shows strong benefits, but they are uneven and matched by new harms; comparisons across contexts depend on the criteria used.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: telemedicine, wearables and digital records improve access and care; disease surveillance and research. Arguments against: mental-health harms from social media; health-data privacy breaches; unequal access. Supported judgement: Health shows strong benefits, but they are uneven and matched by new harms; comparisons across contexts depend on the criteria used. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that statistical sources are more reliable than personal testimony.
items.answer: Statistics show scale and testimony shows experience; reliability depends on method and origin, not type.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: represent many cases and show scale; less influenced by individual emotion. Arguments against: statistics depend on definitions and collection methods; can be selectively presented; testimony captures experiences and causes statistics miss. Supported judgement: Statistics show scale and testimony shows experience; reliability depends on method and origin, not type. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that gig-economy platforms have given workers more freedom than traditional employment.
items.answer: Platforms offer flexibility, but algorithmic control and weak protections mean freedom is often limited; regulation is reshaping the balance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: flexible hours and easy entry to work; income opportunities for migrants and students. Arguments against: algorithmic management controls pay and access to jobs; lack of sick pay, pensions and protection; courts (Uber v Aslam) and the EU Platform Work Directive (2024) recognise imbalance. Supported judgement: Platforms offer flexibility, but algorithmic control and weak protections mean freedom is often limited; regulation is reshaping the balance. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.
